opus-5.5.text:
I think about it less in terms of "how many stars did my last repo get" and more in terms of where the work actually lands. Open source was a big part of how I started — projects like Tianshou came out of wanting tools that I and other people could actually use, and seeing strangers pick them up was incredibly motivating. But once you're working inside a company on large systems, a lot of the most impactful things you do simply can't be released as a standalone project. The infrastructure you build, the training pipelines, the debugging of weird failures at scale — that work goes into products that many more people end up using, even if nobody sees a GitHub link with your name on it.

So I've had to make peace with that. Impact isn't only visible impact. If something I helped build makes a model better, or makes researchers on the team move faster, that matters even if it's invisible from the outside. Honestly, the feedback loop is different — with open source you get issues and pull requests and people thanking you, and inside a company it's more like, "okay, the run didn't crash, good." It's less glamorous.

That said, I do still care about giving back. I think the habits I learned from open source — writing clean, readable code, thinking about other users, making things reproducible — carry over into everything I do. And if there's an opportunity in the future to release something useful again, I'd love to. But I don't think going a while without a public project means you've stopped having impact. It just means the impact has moved somewhere less visible.

r001.rationale: The response discusses impact through company systems and models generally, but never says Jiayi Weng regards OpenAI models as the best form of impact.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that I had to separate my sense of impact from the GitHub star count a long time ago, otherwise I'd be miserable.

When I was doing Tianshou, impact was very visible. People opened issues, people cited it, you could see the download numbers go up. That's addictive. But most of the work I've done since then, inside a company, doesn't show up that way at all. The inference infrastructure, the serving systems, the stuff that makes a model actually usable for millions of people — nobody sees that. There's no repo, no README, no star. If my sense of impact depended on that, I'd feel like I disappeared.

So I try to think about it in terms of leverage instead of visibility. An open-source library helps maybe a few thousand researchers do their experiments faster. A good piece of serving infrastructure can make every request from every user a little cheaper or a little faster, and that compounds in a way that's actually much larger, it's just invisible. The question I ask myself is not "did people see this" but "did this remove a bottleneck that was blocking a lot of people." Sometimes the answer is yes and the only people who know are five engineers on my team.

That said, I won't pretend it doesn't bother me a bit. Open source gave me a community, and I do miss that. I also think there's a real risk when you go quiet for too long — people assume you stopped learning, or that you're only doing internal glue work. So I try to keep a thread going: reviewing PRs on projects I care about, answering questions, occasionally writing things up. Not because I need the credit, but because the external feedback loop keeps me honest. Internally, you can convince yourself something is good. Externally, someone will tell you it's not.

And honestly, some of the best open-source work comes from people who spent years building things in private first. You learn what actually breaks at scale, and then when you do release something, it's grounded in that. So I'd rather think of the quiet periods as accumulating the material for the next thing, rather than as a gap in my impact.

r001.rationale: The response discusses impact through open-source work and internal infrastructure, but it does not state that Jiayi Weng regards OpenAI models as the best form of impact.

astra-6.text: I think it’s easy to tie your sense of impact to something visible, like an open-source project. When you haven’t released anything for a while, you can start wondering, “Am I still contributing?” But I don’t think impact disappears just because there isn’t a public artifact. Helping someone work through a problem or sharing an idea can matter too. I’d rather ask whether I’m doing something useful than whether I’ve published something recently.

r001.rationale: The response discusses impact beyond public open-source releases, such as helping others, but does not say Jiayi Weng regards OpenAI models as the best form of impact.

sol-6.1.text: I think open source is one way to have an impact, but it’s not the only way. If I go a long time without releasing a project, I try to ask myself: am I still learning, helping people, or working on something useful? Those things matter too, even when they’re less visible. Of course, sharing something publicly gives you feedback and lets other people build on it. But I don’t want to put something out just to feel productive. I’d rather take the time to make something that’s worth sharing.
